materializing the conflict as a workaround for write skew
Snapshot isolation's own guarantee is per-row: a write-write conflict on the same row is caught, but nothing about the mechanism inspects any constraint spanning two different rows.

Read skew (topic 11's A5A) and lost update (topic 11's P4) are both prevented by SI's own snapshot: once every read inside a transaction comes from one fixed point in time, neither anomaly's own precondition (a stale read mixed with a fresh one, or two writers racing off the same stale read) can occur.

Write skew needs two disjoint writes and a constraint that spans both rows together; SI's own conflict detection only ever looks at whether a row you wrote was changed since your snapshot, which is why two different rows never trigger it.

Vendor naming is not a technical detail; calling snapshot isolation "serializable" (Oracle) or offering it as the default under a name (REPEATABLE READ) that the SQL standard defines more weakly (Postgres, MySQL) is exactly how an application engineer ends up trusting a guarantee the engine never actually promised.

Materializing the conflict (a dummy row or a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a shared resource) only closes the specific case it is written for; a new query pattern that reads the same invariant a different way can reopen the same anomaly, which is why the field needs a general guarantee, not a list of patches.

The read-only transaction anomaly (named in topic 11, not re-reproduced here) survives snapshot isolation for the same root reason write skew does: a read-only transaction's own snapshot can still be inconsistent with the actual commit order of transactions it never conflicts with.

Two genuinely different mechanisms both close this exact gap without reverting to simple locking: Serializable Snapshot Isolation, which adds anomaly detection on top of SI itself, and strict two-phase locking, which blocks instead of detecting after the fact — the subject of the next topic.

A write-write conflict failing at commit time (SI) is a structurally different event from a lock wait (topic 11's row locking): the second transaction's statement itself succeeds under SI, and only the commit fails, whereas a lock wait blocks the statement itself before it can even run.

items.item: The hook's own doctors scenario passes every individual check (each transaction's own read of the count is accurate, each transaction's own update is valid) — the invariant breaks only when both commits are considered together, which is exactly why no single transaction's own logic can be blamed.

Postgres offers REPEATABLE READ (SI) and SERIALIZABLE (SSI, topic 13's subject) as two distinct levels precisely because SI alone cannot be upgraded to full serializability just by reading more carefully; it needs genuinely different bookkeeping (predicate locks, in Postgres's own case).
